facts.claim: Thrice released the single "Open Your Eyes and Dream" on September 20, 2022, through Epitaph.
Audiomack's metadata lists Thrice as the producer and Epitaph as the label.
Dustin Kensrue said the song is about how big systemic issues feel unchangeable because people have lived with them all their lives, and that this feeling of inevitability is an illusion.
Kensrue said the song is about opening our eyes to the fact that most things seem impossible until they happen, and being willing to dream something better into existence.
The lyrics deal with myths of meritocracy, low wages and calls for change being met with violence. The chorus urges listeners to devise a solidarity.
The track runs about 4:02. Its ISRC is USEP42226003.
A lyric video was released alongside the single.
The band is Dustin Kensrue, Riley Breckenridge, guitarist Teppei Teranishi and bassist Eddie Breckenridge.
The single followed the September 2021 album Horizons/East. The band produced and recorded that album at their own New Grass Studio, and Scott Evans mixed it.
Thrice formed in 1998 in Irvine, California. Wikipedia's discography lists this song as a non-album single.

research.lineage: Thrice are an Orange County, California band described by press as post-hardcore natives, and this single pairs a restrained alternative verse with a heavy post-hardcore chorus.

draft:
The verb in the chorus is the strangest and best choice on **Open Your Eyes and Dream**. Thrice don't ask you to hope for solidarity or wait for it. They ask you to devise one, as if it were a machine you could draw up and build. The whole song turns on that idea: what feels permanent was made by someone, so it can be remade.

The verses earn the turn by sitting in exhaustion first. "Marred by myths of meritocracy" packs a whole argument into a tongue-twisting line. The ladder is a story, and the few who climb it get held up as proof that everyone could. The second verse gets more physical: sweating in the swelter, swallowing rage, breaking backs for half a living wage. Then comes the sharpest image here: "We've watched this film too often." The narrator isn't naive about any of this. The feeling is a tired, knowing anger, the kind that has seen calls for change met with violence and stopped expecting a plot twist.

That weariness never fully goes away, and the hope doesn't cancel it. They sit side by side. Dustin Kensrue has said the song is about how big systemic problems feel unchangeable because we've lived with them our whole lives, and how that sense of inevitability is an illusion. Most things, he said, seem impossible until they happen. The bridge line, "Knowing nothing has to be like this," carries that idea, and the lyric repeats it four times in a row with an echo of "be like this" trailing behind. It reads like someone talking themselves out of despair, one repetition at a time.

The band plays it with urgency. A distorted electric guitar runs a fast, arpeggiated riff over a bass line that pushes from below, and the drums lock into a steady mid-tempo beat with a hard snare and kick. The groove keeps moving forward. The vocal comes in clear and melodic with a little grit at the edges. It holds its notes instead of barking them, and there are no harmonies to soften it. The production is clean, and a moderate room sound keeps every part distinct.

This is the Orange County post-hardcore that Thrice came out of in 1998, aimed outward. The urgency of that scene points at wages and myths rather than heartbreak. Here Thrice self-produced the song, with guitarist Teppei Teranishi and bassist Eddie Breckenridge alongside Kensrue and drummer Riley Breckenridge.

The song lets you keep your anger and your hope in the same hand, and by the fourth "nothing has to be like this," you start to believe it a little.

factCheck.claim: The chorus verb is 'devise' ('Devise a solidarity'), and Thrice ask listeners to devise one.
factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics. The machine image is interpretation.
Exact lyric. The 'ladder' reading is interpretation.

factCheck.claim: Second verse: sweating in the swelter, swallowing rage, breaking backs for half a living wage.

factCheck.note: Exact lyric. The narrator reading rests on 'Stop waiting for a twist' and 'Our calls for change / Are always answered with violence.'
